chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) ruled in the case of a man against whom two men testified that he had stolen, so his hand was cut off. Then afterwards, the two witnesses came with another man and said, 'This is the thief, and not the one whose hand was cut off; we merely likened this one to that one.' So he ruled against them that their compensation was half the blood money, and he did not validate their testimony against the other man.

key_terms.لَمْ يُجِزْ شَهَادَتَهُمَا: He did not validate/accept their testimony

ai.seo_question: What is the legal consequence for witnesses who testify to a theft but later admit they made a mistake in identifying the thief?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the principle of 'gharamah' (financial compensation for judicial error) in Shia jurisprudence, where witnesses bear the cost of their mistake when their testimony leads to an unjust punishment. Imam Ali (AS) ruled that the two witnesses must pay half the blood money (diyah) for the amputated hand, highlighting the severity of relying on probable identification ('shabah') rather than certainty. This ruling underscores the high standard of proof required in hudud cases and the financial liability of witnesses for errors in identification.
